title: FIFA’s solution to empty World Cup luxury seats? Give them to volunteers
content:
The first game at Dallas Cowboys’ AT&T Stadium was always going to be a revealing case study for the tournament’s attendance situation.

A cavernous venue, two high-profile, competitive sides, in a large and sports-hungry North Texas market, easily accessible by most international flights.

On paper, the ingredients were there for a rousing full house in Arlington, Texas.

And at first glance, that is more or less what it looked like. The upper levels were largely filled out, and the atmosphere was loud. There were no glaring, patchwork absences that had been so visible in Guadalajara two days earlier.

But a close look at the hospitality boxes behind each goal drew the eye. During NFL and college football games, these slightly-above field-level sections are paid tickets, known as the touchdown suites. There are 14 of these in total at AT&T. Here’s a typical view from the seats when the Dallas Cowboys are in action.

But during pregame ceremonies for this World Cup game between Netherlands and Japan, the touchdown suites were pretty much empty. They were not listed on general sale to the public for this tournament but prices were available on request.

And they remained vacant in the opening stages of the match, too.

Then, roughly 10 minutes into the game, the seats were suddenly full — not with paying supporters, but with volunteers in their neon-green hi-vis clothing. At least one area of the section on the southwest side had some regular fans, but the rest on both sides were full of event volunteers.

FIFA volunteers inside the stadium told The Athletic that those helping with the pregame ceremony had been allowed to occupy the unsold hospitality seats “as a treat.”

The Athletic understands that to be the case — sources with knowledge of the matter confirmed that the sections had failed to attract buyers, with only three of the 14 available suites sold. Volunteers were relocated to occupy the remaining seats.

FIFA subsequently posted a video to its social channels of the moment the volunteers (some of whom had been giving up their free time since November) were told they would be watching the game from those seats.

But why did the hospitality tickets behind the goals not sell?

One explanation may be an unusual architectural quirk specific to this venue. The AT&T Stadium field was raised about four feet to accommodate the soccer pitch, which brings the netting, photographers, and cameras more level with the sightlines than the American football set-up.

Of course, it’s also possible that those luxury suites for this Netherlands-Japan game just did not sell beyond the three, given the costs that would have been involved.

On the attendance figures, FIFA’s position mirrors the one it offered after Guadalajara: “Official attendance figures reflect the number of tickets scanned, and spectators present within the stadium footprint, rather than visual assessments of seating occupancy at any given moment during the game.

“FIFA works closely with stadium authorities and ticketing teams to ensure all published figures are based on verified operational data.”

Volunteer-occupied seats are not included in that count. The official attendance was 69,285, which means there were officially 1,364 empty seats at Dallas Stadium. That is the most of any 2026 World Cup game so far, according to FIFA’s numbers.
